newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS-Portuguese cement firms to invest abroad.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Portuguese cement firms to invest abroad.

text.p: A burst of construction activity is boosting cash flow of Portugal's cement firms, but they must invest abroad to maximise returns and make up for an expected flattening in domestic demand after the 1998 Lisbon World Fair, analysts said.

Plentiful public works projects in the run-up to December local elections and intensive building for the Lisbon Expo, as well as favourable weather conditions ensured that demand for cement would rise at least five percent this year, they said.

Cash-rich Cimpor-Cimentos de Portugal, the biggest cement company, was absorbing recent acquisitions in Brazil and Morocco and prowling for further foreign plants to maximise returns and growth prospects, they added.
Pedro Fonseca of UBS in London said he expected Cimpor's share price to rise by around 10 percent between now and the end of 1997 as it caught up with the BVL General share index.
He forecast Earnings Per Share (EPS) of 167 escudos in 1997, 251 in 1998 and 293 in 1999.
Cimpor shares have risen by some 23 percent this year, while the BVL index has surged by 40 percent.
Cimpor shares rose 23 escudos to 4,151 in afternoon trade on Lisbon bourse in volume of 206,828 shares.
James Harrison of Lisbon broker Midas said he had set a price target of 4,500 escudos per share for Cimpor by the end of 1997. Midas rates Cimpor a "Buy".
Harrison forecast cash flow per share of 509 escudos in 1997 and 531 in 1998, up from 483 in 1996.
"Cimpor has underperformed the market because of uncertainties over the Brazilian acquisitions," he said.

In January, Cimpor acquired CISAFRA, a cement producer, and the SERRANA group's cement business, for 62 billion escudos. The companies together account for five percent of the growing Brazilian market.

The managing director of Portugal's other cement holding, Semapa-SGPS, Carlos Alves, said last month that his group expected to boost its consolidated sales by around six percent in 1997 as both demand for cement and prices increased.
He also said Semapa was looking to invest in cement production abroad, but had no immediate plans.
Analysts were bearish on Semapa, as its small size made it hard for the company to compete with much larger international cement groups to buy foreign plants. UBS rates Semapa a "Sell".
"If there were a price war for a plant, Semapa would struggle to compete with the industry's giants," said Fonseca.
Semapa shares stood at 4,315 escudos, up 35, in volume of 16,600 shares in afternoon trade on Lisbon bourse.

Despite expectations that growth in domestic demand will halt after Expo, some analysts said that the present climate of falling interest rates and enthusiastic demand for mortgages could eventually lift orders for new housing.
A strong pound against the escudo was boosting interest by British investors in construction projects in the southern holiday Algarve region. - - Lisbon newsroom +351-1-3538254
